modules.title: Basic Sentence Structure
modules.description: Learn the fundamental particles and verb forms that form the backbone of every Japanese sentence.

lessons.title: は (wa) Particle
lessons.description: Master the topic marker particle は and the basic AはBです pattern.

body.html:
The particle は (pronounced wa, not ha) marks the topic of a sentence — the thing you are talking about.

The most basic Japanese sentence pattern is:

A は B です。
A wa B desu.
"A is B."

Examples:

  • わたしは がくせい です。 — I am a student.
  • これは ほん です。 — This is a book.
  • たなかさんは にほんじん です。 — Tanaka-san is Japanese.

To make it negative, replace です with じゃないです (or the more formal ではありません):

  • わたしは がくせい じゃないです。 — I am not a student.
tips: は is written with the hiragana は (ha) but pronounced 'wa' when used as a particle.
です (desu) makes the sentence polite. In casual speech it can be dropped.
The topic is often omitted when it is obvious from context.

body.question: わたし ＿ がくせい です。 (I am a student.)
body.explanation: は (wa) is the topic marker. It marks わたし (I) as the topic of the sentence: 'As for me, (I) am a student.'

lessons.title: が (ga) Particle
lessons.description: Learn the subject marker particle が and how it differs from は, including its use with existence verbs.

body.html:
The particle が (ga) marks the subject of a sentence. While は marks what you're talking about, が identifies who or what performs the action or exists.

Key uses of が:

  1. New information / answering "who/what":
    だれが きましたか。 — Who came?
    たなかさんが きました。 — Tanaka-san came.
  2. Existence verbs (いる / ある):
    ねこが います。 — There is a cat.
    つくえの うえに ほんが あります。 — There is a book on the desk.
  3. Likes / abilities (すき / できる):
    わたしは すしが すきです。 — I like sushi.

は vs が: は sets the scene ("as for X..."), while が spotlights the subject ("X is the one that...").
tips: Use います (imasu) for living things (people, animals) and あります (arimasu) for non-living things.
が often answers questions with だれ (who) or なに (what).
With adjectives like すき (like) and じょうず (good at), the object of the feeling takes が, not を.

body.question: へやに ねこ が ＿。 (There is a cat in the room.)
body.explanation: います (imasu) is used for living things. Since a cat (ねこ) is a living creature, we use います.

body.sentence: つくえの うえに ほん ___ あります。
body.explanation: が marks the subject of the existence verb あります. 'There is a book on the desk.'

lessons.title: を (wo) Particle
lessons.description: Learn the direct object marker を and how to use it with transitive verbs.

body.html:
The particle を (pronounced o) marks the direct object — the thing that receives the action of a verb.

Pattern: Subject は Object を Verb。

Examples:

  • わたしは みずを のみます。 — I drink water.
  • ほんを よみます。 — (I) read a book.
  • にほんごを べんきょうします。 — (I) study Japanese.
  • テレビを みます。 — (I) watch TV.

を is only used with transitive verbs — verbs that take a direct object (eat, drink, read, buy, etc.).
tips: を is written with the hiragana を (wo) but pronounced 'o' in modern Japanese.
Intransitive verbs (go, come, sleep) do NOT take を.
を also marks a place you move through: こうえんを あるきます (I walk through the park).

body.sentence: まいにち しんぶん ___ よみます。
body.explanation: を marks しんぶん (newspaper) as the direct object of よみます (read). 'I read the newspaper every day.'

lessons.title: Verb Conjugation: ます Form
lessons.description: Learn the polite present/future verb form used in everyday conversation.

body.html:
The ます form (masu-form) is the polite way to conjugate verbs in Japanese. It is the standard form used in daily conversation with people you are not very close to.

Conjugation patterns:

FormSuffixExample (たべる → eat)
Present affirmative〜ますたべます (I eat / I will eat)
Present negative〜ませんたべません (I don't eat)
Past affirmative〜ましたたべました (I ate)
Past negative〜ませんでしたたべませんでした (I didn't eat)

Common ます-form verbs:

  • いきます (go) / きます (come) / かえります (return)
  • たべます (eat) / のみます (drink) / みます (see, watch)
  • よみます (read) / かきます (write) / ききます (listen)
  • はなします (speak) / べんきょうします (study)
tips: ます form does not distinguish between present and future — context decides.
Japanese verbs do not change for person or number: たべます means I/you/he/she/we/they eat.
To say 'let's do X', change ます to ましょう: たべましょう (let's eat).

body.question: きのう テレビを ＿。 (I did not watch TV yesterday.)
body.explanation: みませんでした is the past negative form of みます. きのう (yesterday) tells us it is past tense, and the English indicates it is negative.

body.question: いっしょに ひるごはんを ＿。 (Let's eat lunch together.)
body.explanation: たべましょう is the volitional form ('let's eat'). Change ます to ましょう to suggest doing something together.

flashcardDecks.title: Essential N5 Grammar Points
flashcardDecks.description: 25 fundamental grammar points every N5 learner must know, covering particles, verb forms, and basic sentence patterns.

back.example: わたしは がくせいです。(I am a student.)
back.notes: Written は but pronounced 'wa' as a particle.

back.example: ねこが います。(There is a cat.)
back.notes: Marks the grammatical subject; used with existence verbs and adjectives like すき.

back.example: みずを のみます。(I drink water.)
back.notes: Written を but pronounced 'o'. Marks what receives the verb's action.

back.example: がっこうに いきます。(I go to school.)
back.notes: Indicates direction, specific time, or location of existence.

back.example: としょかんで べんきょうします。(I study at the library.)
back.notes: Marks where an action takes place or the means/tool used.

back.example: にほんへ いきます。(I go to Japan.)
back.notes: Written へ but pronounced 'e'. Indicates direction of movement, interchangeable with に for destinations.

back.example: ともだちと いきます。(I go with a friend.)
back.notes: Connects nouns exhaustively ('A and B') or marks a companion.

back.example: わたしも がくせいです。(I am also a student.)
back.notes: Replaces は, が, or を to mean 'also'.

back.example: これは なんですか。(What is this?)
back.notes: Added to the end of a sentence to form a question. Replaces the period.

back.example: わたしの ほん。(My book.)
back.notes: Connects two nouns: the first modifies the second.

back.example: がくせいです。(I am a student.)
back.notes: Makes a statement polite. Negative: じゃないです / ではありません.

back.example: たべます。(I eat. / I will eat.)
back.notes: Negative: ません. Past: ました. Past negative: ませんでした.

back.example: のみません。(I don't drink.)
back.notes: Present negative of ます-form verbs.

back.example: いきました。(I went.)
back.notes: Past affirmative of ます-form verbs.

back.example: たべましょう。(Let's eat.)
back.notes: Used to suggest doing something together.

back.example: すしを たべたいです。(I want to eat sushi.)
back.notes: Attach to the ます-stem. Conjugates like an い-adjective.

back.example: ほんを よんでいます。(I am reading a book.)
back.notes: Polite form: ています. Shows ongoing action or resulting state.

back.example: みてください。(Please look.)
back.notes: て-form + ください. Polite request.

back.example: たばこを すわないでください。(Please don't smoke.)
back.notes: ない-form + でください. Polite negative request.

back.example: ここに すわってもいいですか。(May I sit here?)
back.notes: て-form + もいいです. Asks or grants permission.

back.example: ここで たべてはいけません。(You must not eat here.)
back.notes: て-form + はいけません. States a prohibition.

back.example: にほんは フランスより ちいさいです。(Japan is smaller than France.)
back.notes: より marks the thing being compared against.

back.example: くじから ごじまで はたらきます。(I work from 9 to 5.)
back.notes: Can indicate time or place. Often used together.

back.example: おんがくが すきです。(I like music.)
back.notes: The object of liking takes が, not を. Negative: すきじゃないです.

back.example: あたらしい くるまが ほしいです。(I want a new car.)
back.notes: Used for wanting things (nouns). For wanting to do actions, use 〜たい.

modules.title: First Words
modules.description: Build your first Japanese vocabulary with essential words for everyday life.

lessons.title: Self-Introduction
lessons.description: Learn the key words you need to introduce yourself in Japanese.

body.html:
Self-introduction (じこしょうかい) is one of the first things you will do in Japanese. Here are the key words:

  • わたし — I, me
  • なまえ (名前) — name
  • くに (国) — country
  • ねんれい (年齢) — age
  • しごと (仕事) — job, work
  • がくせい (学生) — student

Example self-introduction:

はじめまして。わたしの なまえは マリアです。アメリカから きました。にじゅうさんさいです。だいがくせいです。どうぞ よろしく おねがいします。

Nice to meet you. My name is Maria. I came from America. I am 23 years old. I am a university student. Pleased to meet you.
tips: わたし is gender-neutral. Men sometimes use ぼく (boku) in casual speech.
〜から きました means 'I came from ~' — a standard way to state your country.
どうぞ よろしく おねがいします is a set phrase with no direct English equivalent.

body.question: What does なまえ (名前) mean?
body.explanation: なまえ (名前) means 'name'. わたしの なまえ = my name.

body.sentence: わたしの ___ は たなかです。
body.explanation: なまえ (名前) means 'name'. わたしの なまえは たなかです = My name is Tanaka.

lessons.title: Family Members
lessons.description: Learn how to talk about your family and ask about others' families.

body.html:
Japanese has two sets of family words: humble forms (for your own family) and honorific forms (for someone else's family).

RelationOwn familySomeone else's
Motherはは (haha)おかあさん (okaasan)
Fatherちち (chichi)おとうさん (otousan)
Older sisterあね (ane)おねえさん (oneesan)
Older brotherあに (ani)おにいさん (oniisan)
Younger sisterいもうと (imouto)いもうとさん (imoutosan)
Younger brotherおとうと (otouto)おとうとさん (otoutosan)
Siblingsきょうだい (kyoudai)

Example:

  • わたしの ははは いしゃです。 — My mother is a doctor.
  • おかあさんは おげんきですか。 — Is your mother well?
tips: Use humble forms (はは, ちち) when talking about YOUR family to others.
Use honorific forms (おかあさん, おとうさん) when referring to SOMEONE ELSE's family or when addressing your own parents directly.
かぞく (家族) is the general word for 'family'.

body.question: When talking about your own mother to someone else, which word should you use?
body.explanation: はは (haha) is the humble form used when referring to your own mother in conversation with others. おかあさん is for someone else's mother or when addressing your own mother directly.

lessons.title: Food & Drink
lessons.description: Learn essential food and drink vocabulary for restaurants and daily meals.

body.html:
Here are essential words for food and drink at the N5 level:

Staples & Meals:

  • ごはん (御飯) — rice / meal
  • パン — bread
  • たまご (卵) — egg

Ingredients:

  • にく (肉) — meat
  • さかな (魚) — fish
  • やさい (野菜) — vegetables
  • くだもの (果物) — fruit

Drinks:

  • みず (水) — water
  • おちゃ (お茶) — tea
  • コーヒー — coffee
  • ぎゅうにゅう (牛乳) — milk

Example sentences:

  • あさごはんに たまごを たべます。 — I eat eggs for breakfast.
  • おちゃを のみませんか。 — Won't you have some tea?
tips: ごはん can mean both 'cooked rice' and 'meal' depending on context.
あさごはん = breakfast, ひるごはん = lunch, ばんごはん = dinner.
Many food loanwords use katakana: コーヒー, パン, サラダ, etc.

body.question: Which word means 'vegetables'?
body.explanation: やさい (野菜) means 'vegetables'. くだもの = fruit, さかな = fish, にく = meat.

body.sentence: まいあさ ___ を のみます。
body.explanation: Many answers are possible. みず (水) means 'water'. まいあさ みずを のみます = I drink water every morning.

lessons.title: Daily Objects
lessons.description: Learn the names of everyday objects you see and use constantly.

body.html:
Here are common everyday objects you will encounter:

  • ほん (本) — book
  • かばん (鞄) — bag
  • でんわ (電話) — telephone
  • とけい (時計) — clock, watch
  • かさ (傘) — umbrella
  • かぎ (鍵) — key
  • さいふ (財布) — wallet
  • めがね (眼鏡) — glasses
  • ノート — notebook
  • えんぴつ (鉛筆) — pencil
  • ペン — pen

Useful pattern:

これは ＿ です。 — This is a ＿.

  • これは わたしの かばんです。 — This is my bag.
  • あれは たなかさんの とけいです。 — That (over there) is Tanaka-san's watch.
tips: でんわ originally means 'telephone' but けいたいでんわ or スマホ is used for mobile phones.
とけい can be a wall clock or a wristwatch — context clarifies.
Use これ (this), それ (that near you), あれ (that over there) to point at objects.

body.question: とけい (時計) means:
body.explanation: とけい (時計) means 'clock' or 'watch'. でんわ = telephone, かさ = umbrella, かぎ = key.

modules.title: Essential Expressions
modules.description: Learn the key phrases and expressions you need for basic communication in Japanese.

lessons.title: Greetings
lessons.description: Master the essential Japanese greetings for every time of day and situation.

body.html:
Japanese greetings change depending on the time of day and the level of formality.

Time-based greetings:

  • おはようございます — Good morning (polite)
    Casual: おはよう
  • こんにちは — Good afternoon / Hello
  • こんばんは — Good evening

Parting expressions:

  • さようなら — Goodbye (somewhat formal)
  • じゃあね / またね — See you (casual)
  • おやすみなさい — Good night (polite)
    Casual: おやすみ

Other essentials:

  • ありがとうございます — Thank you (polite)
  • すみません — Excuse me / I'm sorry
  • おねがいします — Please (when requesting)
tips: こんにちは and こんばんは end with は (wa particle), not わ.
おはよう is very casual — use おはようございます with teachers, bosses, strangers.
すみません works as both 'excuse me' (to get attention) and 'I'm sorry' (for minor apologies).

body.question: It's 8:00 AM and you meet your teacher. What do you say?
body.explanation: おはようございます is the polite morning greeting. Use it with teachers, colleagues, and people you are not close to.
ありがとうございます is the polite form of 'thank you'. ございます adds politeness.

lessons.title: At a Shop
lessons.description: Learn essential expressions for shopping and buying things in Japan.

body.html:
These phrases will help you navigate shops and restaurants in Japan.

Pointing at things:

  • これ — this (near me)
  • それ — that (near you)
  • あれ — that (over there)
  • どれ — which one?

Key expressions:

  • いくらですか。 — How much is it?
  • これを ください。 — This one, please. / I'll take this.
  • 〜を みせてください。 — Please show me ~.
  • カードで いいですか。 — Is card (payment) okay?

Sample dialogue:

You: すみません、これは いくらですか。
Shop: さんびゃくえんです。
You: じゃ、これを ください。

You: Excuse me, how much is this?
Shop: It's 300 yen.
You: Then, I'll take this please.
tips: ください literally means 'please give me' — it's the standard way to order or buy.
これ/それ/あれ are pronouns (this one). この/その/あの are adjectives (this ~, that ~).
いくら (how much) should not be confused with イクラ (salmon roe)!

body.question: You want to point at something far away from both you and the listener. Which word do you use?
body.explanation: あれ (are) refers to something far from both the speaker and the listener. これ = near speaker, それ = near listener, どれ = which one.

lessons.title: Asking Questions
lessons.description: Learn the essential question words to ask about people, places, things, and time.

body.html:
Japanese question words (interrogatives) are essential for gathering information. Unlike English, word order does not change in questions — you simply place the question word where the answer would go and add か at the end.

Key question words:

  • なに / なん (何) — what
    これは なんですか。 — What is this?
  • だれ (誰) — who
    だれが きましたか。 — Who came?
  • どこ — where
    トイレは どこですか。 — Where is the restroom?
  • いつ — when
    いつ いきますか。 — When will you go?
  • どう — how
    にほんは どうですか。 — How is Japan?
  • なぜ / どうして — why
    どうして にほんごを べんきょうしますか。 — Why do you study Japanese?
  • いくつ — how many / how old
    りんごは いくつ ありますか。 — How many apples are there?
tips: なに becomes なん before です, で, and counters: なんですか, なんにん.
Japanese questions keep the same word order as statements — just swap the unknown with the question word.
In polite speech, always end questions with か. In casual speech, か can be replaced by rising intonation.

body.explanation: どこ means 'where'. トイレは どこですか = Where is the restroom? — one of the most useful questions in Japan.

body.question: You want to ask 'Who is that person?' — あのひとは ＿ ですか。 Which word fills the blank?
body.explanation: だれ (dare) means 'who'. あのひとは だれですか = Who is that person?

back.example: すみません、えきは どこですか。(Excuse me, where is the station?)
back.notes: Used to get attention AND for light apologies

back.example: コーヒーを おねがいします。(Coffee, please.)

back.notes: Used only at the FIRST meeting

front.reading: どうぞ よろしく おねがいします

back.text: Pleased to meet you / Please treat me well
back.example: End of a self-introduction
back.notes: No direct English equivalent; a standard closing for introductions

back.example: これは いくらですか。(How much is this?)
back.notes: Essential shopping phrase

back.example: これを ください。(This one, please.)
back.notes: Used for ordering, buying, or requesting something

front.text: これ / それ / あれ
front.reading: これ / それ / あれ

back.example: これは なんですか。(What is this?)
back.notes: こ = near speaker, そ = near listener, あ = far from both

back.example: これは なんですか。(What is this?)
back.notes: なに → なん before です

back.example: あのひとは だれですか。(Who is that person?)
back.notes: More polite: どなたですか

back.example: トイレは どこですか。(Where is the restroom?)
back.notes: One of the most useful travel phrases

back.example: しけんは いつですか。(When is the exam?)
back.notes: いつ does not need a particle

back.example: はい、わかりました。(Yes, I understand.)
back.notes: Past form used to confirm understanding. Negative: わかりません (I don't understand)

front.text: もういちど おねがいします
front.reading: もういちど おねがいします

back.example: Asking someone to repeat what they said
back.notes: Very useful for language learners

back.text: It's okay / I'm fine / No thank you
back.example: レシートは? — だいじょうぶです。(Receipt? — No, thank you.)
back.notes: Context-dependent: can mean 'I'm fine', 'it's okay', or politely decline
